newsitem.title: IRAQ: More foreign firms line up to buy Iraqi crude oil.
newsitem.headline: More foreign firms line up to buy Iraqi crude oil.

text.p: Foreign firms are still lining up to buy Iraqi crude oil despite assertions that contracts signed so far account for all the oil the United Nations allows Iraq to sell in the next six months, a senior Iraqi oil official said on Sunday.

Demand for Iraqi crude far exceeded the quantities Iraq could sell under its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations which set a six-month revenue ceiling of $2 billion, the official from Iraq's State Organisation for the Marketing of Oil (SOMO), who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
Rising oil prices meant that Iraq had to lower its average amount of sales under the plan to 550,000 barrels per day (bpd) from an initial estimate of 750,000 bpd, he said.

"They are coming with their briefcases, driving all the way from Amman to Baghdad. We receive them all and sign tentative deals. Our policy is to keep in touch with our former clients," The official said.
He did not name the companies and did not disclose the number of contracts signed since the deal went into effect on December 10.
SOMO could easily find customers willing to buy up to three million bpd if allowed unrestrained exports, he said.
The oil-for-food deal is designed to ease the impact of stringent trade sanctions imposed on Iraq in August 1990 when its troops invaded Kuwait.
Industry and U.N. sources said on Friday the United Nations was holding up approval of some contracts submitted by Iraq, concerned that Baghdad's deals may exceed the $2 billion limit.

So far 16 contracts have been approved by oil experts or overseers hired by the United Nations. But according to oil industry sources SOMO has signed contracts with at least four other companies and is in negotiations with another three.
Iraq puts its current production capacity at 2.5 million bpd and says it can be boosted to three million in three months. It exported three million bpd before invading Kuwait in 1990.
"The quality of our crude is needed in many places in the world. There are many refineries especially designed for our oil," the SOMO official said.

The six-month oil-for-food deal is renewable. Removal of all curbs on Iraqi oil exports needs testimony from the U.N. Special Commission that Baghdad had done all that required from it under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire on disarmament.

A technical fault held up Iraqi exports via pipeline to Turkey for about 48 hours after they were personally unleashed by President Saddam Hussein on December 10. Since then Iraq has been pumping about 350,000 bpd for export via the Turkish terminal of Ceyhan and up to 250,000 from a Gulf port.
Several supertankers have sailed with crude loaded at Ceyhan or the Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr and SOMO officials said they expected the flow to continue with no difficulty.
One official said requirements set by U.N. oil overseers for monitoring exports through both routes were "harsh and something unheard-of in oil industry but our experts were up to the challenge".
"I say this because many betted on this. There is no propaganda for things like the export ability. There is no need to exaggerate it up or down...Sooner or later you will be discovered," he said.
